messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Jamal, a 58-year-old African American man who had spent most of his adult life cutting hair in a small neighborhood salon, came to treatment after his wife said she no longer recognized how withdrawn and tense he had become. The robbery had happened just after closing one winter evening, when he was locking up the shop and counting the day’s cash by the counter. Two men approached from the alley, one of them smelling strongly of alcohol before either spoke, and their manner shifted from uncertain to threatening in a way Jamal still described as suspicious, like they were circling him and deciding what to do. One shoved him against the wall, demanded the money, and struck him hard enough to leave him stunned; what stayed with Jamal most was not a neat story he could tell, but flashes of the men’s faces, the glint of the knife, his own hands dropping the bills, and the sound of his wife’s voice in his head later asking how it had happened so fast. He said he knew what happened, but when he tried to explain it, the words would not come; it was all “just pictures,” as if the scene kept arriving in fragments he could not arrange into language. Those pictures replayed like a film over and over, especially at night, and the more they returned, the more he found himself scanning the street for people acting suspiciously and tensing whenever he caught alcohol on someone’s breath or coat. 

In the weeks that followed, Jamal noticed that criticism and correction began to sting in a new way. In the salon, if a customer complained that he had cut too much hair off one side, or if a fellow stylist casually corrected his technique, he felt the same hot rush of shame and danger that had come with the robbery, as though being wrong in front of another person might somehow make him vulnerable again. Those moments sent him back to the alley in his mind: the sudden threat, the shove, the helplessness, the pictures that would not stay still. He came to dread the return of those images, because once they started he would spend hours trying to force them away, clenching his jaw and telling himself not to think about it, not to picture the knife, not to remember the smell of alcohol on the man’s breath. Yet the harder he tried to suppress it, the more forcefully it seemed to break through, and afterward he would dwell on what he had done wrong—whether he should have left the shop earlier, whether he should have looked more alert, whether he had somehow invited it by not being careful enough. That self-blame made him even more watchful in public, and the watchfulness kept the event alive; every suspicious glance on the sidewalk, every man speaking too loudly near the storefront, every whiff of liquor at the end of the day pulled him back into the same frightened state.

By the time he sought help, Jamal had narrowed his life to an effort to avoid other people as much as possible. He stopped lingering after work, no longer accepted invitations from longtime friends, and let his wife handle errands that would have brought him into crowded stores or onto busy blocks. At the salon he still worked, but he kept to the chair, moved quickly between clients, and avoided conversation that might feel like criticism. Even there, with scissors in hand and the familiar smell of shampoo in the air, he watched the door too often, bracing whenever someone entered looking edgy or uncertain. He had come to believe that if he stayed guarded enough and kept his thoughts pushed down, he could prevent the memories from taking over and could avoid the kind of situation that had trapped him once before. Instead, the isolation gave the memories more room to play, and the memories made him more eager to withdraw and more easily startled by the very cues that reminded him of the mugging. By the time his wife insisted he speak to someone, Jamal was exhausted by the loop of fear, blame, and vigilance, and what he wanted most was to stop feeling that every critical remark, every smell of alcohol, and every suspicious stranger meant danger was about to begin again.
